_meta.purpose: A sourced timeline of major POPULATION-SHIFT events readable in ancient DNA — moments where the genetic makeup of a region changed sharply, which is the physical evidence of migration, admixture, replacement, or (sometimes) conquest. Built to answer the user's question: DNA as the 'ultimate truth' of who moved, who mixed, and who was replaced — from Homo sapiens meeting Neanderthals to the layered ancestry of modern South Asians.
_meta.honesty: This is one of the most politicised areas of science. We hold strictly to peer-reviewed ancient-DNA findings (chiefly the Reich lab: Narasimhan et al. 2019 Science; Shinde et al. 2019 Cell) and label clearly where a GENETIC finding (well-established) ends and a HISTORICAL interpretation (contested) begins. A DNA shift proves movement and mixture; it does NOT by itself prove violence — 'migration', 'admixture' and 'conquest' are different claims and we keep them distinct. The 'Aryan migration/invasion' framing is flagged contested precisely here.

key_ancestries.AASI: Ancient Ancestral South Indians — a deeply divergent lineage, distantly related to Andamanese & other early out-of-Africa peoples; the substrate of the subcontinent.
key_ancestries.Iranian_farmer_related: Neolithic ancestry related to farmers of the Iranian plateau; entered South Asia before/around the Indus Valley Civilisation (the IVC individual sequenced was a mix of this + AASI, with NO Steppe or Anatolian farmer ancestry).
key_ancestries.Steppe_pastoralist: Yamnaya-related ancestry from the Pontic-Caspian steppe (the 'Yamnaya' / 'Steppe' people); spread into both Bronze-Age Europe and South Asia ~2000-1500 BCE, up to ~30% of some modern South Asian groups; associated by the authors with Indo-European (incl. Indo-Iranian) languages.
key_ancestries.Neanderthal: ~1.5-2.1% of the DNA of all non-African people today comes from admixture with Neanderthals ~50,000-60,000 years ago.

sources.label: Narasimhan, Patterson et al. (2019), 'The formation of human populations in South and Central Asia', Science 365:eaat7487
Shinde, Narasimhan et al. (2019), 'An Ancient Harappan Genome Lacks Ancestry from Steppe Pastoralists or Iranian Farmers', Cell 179(3):729-735
Reich, D. (2018), 'Who We Are and How We Got Here', Pantheon
Green et al. (2010), 'A Draft Sequence of the Neandertal Genome', Science 328:710-722

events.title: Homo sapiens × Neanderthal admixture (and Neanderthal disappearance)
events.finding: As modern humans left Africa they interbred with Neanderthals; every non-African person alive carries ~1.5–2.1% Neanderthal DNA. Neanderthals then vanished from the record ~40,000 years ago.
events.interpretation: Whether sapiens actively 'killed off' Neanderthals or outcompeted/absorbed them is debated — the DNA proves interbreeding and eventual replacement, but NOT a specific massacre. This is the user's 'sapiens taking over Neanderthals' point, stated at the level the evidence supports: replacement + admixture, mechanism uncertain.
events.note_on_violence: Population replacement in ancient DNA can result from conflict, disease, differential fertility, or absorption — genetics alone rarely distinguishes them.

source.label: Green et al. 2010, Science; subsequent Neanderthal-genome work

events.title: AASI — the deep substrate of South Asia
events.finding: A deeply divergent hunter-gatherer lineage (AASI), distantly related to the Andamanese and other early out-of-Africa peoples, formed the ancient population substrate of the subcontinent — the layer everything later mixed into.
events.interpretation: AASI is not sampled directly (no ancient AASI genome yet) but is inferred as a source in every model of South Asian ancestry.

events.title: Iranian-farmer-related ancestry enters South Asia
events.finding: Ancestry related to Neolithic Iranian-plateau farmers mixed with AASI to form the people of the Indus Valley Civilisation. The single sequenced IVC individual (Rakhigarhi) was exactly this mix — with NO Steppe and NO Anatolian-farmer ancestry.
events.interpretation: This ties living South Asians directly to the IVC population. The absence of Steppe ancestry in the IVC individual is a key data point in the Aryan-migration debate below.

events.title: Steppe (Yamnaya) pastoralist ancestry spreads into South Asia
events.region: Central Asia → NW South Asia (Swat Valley)
events.finding: Steppe (Yamnaya-related) ancestry — the same profile seen spreading into Bronze-Age Europe — reached South Asia in the first half of the 2nd millennium BCE, contributing up to ~30% of the ancestry of some modern groups. Indo-European-speaking groups carry more of it than Dravidian-speaking groups.
events.interpretation: The Reich-lab authors read this as the movement that likely spread Indo-Iranian languages into the subcontinent. THIS is the scientific basis of the 'Aryan migration' picture — see the contested entry.

source.label: Narasimhan et al. 2019, Science (Swat Valley time-transect)

events.title: Formation of the two ancestral populations (ANI & ASI)
events.finding: The IVC-derived population mixed in two directions: southeast (forming the Ancestral South Indians, ASI) and with Steppe-descended groups (forming the Ancestral North Indians, ANI). Almost all South Asians today are a blend of ANI and ASI, whose common thread is the IVC-like ancestry.
events.interpretation: Later the caste system reduced inter-group mixing, 'freezing' distinct ANI/ASI proportions across communities — itself readable in the DNA.

source.label: Reich et al.; Narasimhan et al. 2019

events.title: The 'Aryan migration vs. indigenous origin' interpretation
events.finding: The GENETICS are not seriously disputed: Steppe ancestry entered South Asia ~2000-1500 BCE. What is contested is the HISTORICAL narrative attached to it.
events.interpretation: Mainstream genetics/linguistics reads the Steppe influx as an inward MIGRATION that spread Indo-Aryan languages (a migration, not necessarily a violent 'invasion'). Some Indian scholars/commentators dispute the direction, timing, or the 'Aryan' label, or argue for an indigenous / Out-of-India origin. We present the genetic finding as established and the invasion/indigenous framing as contested — deliberately NOT taking a side beyond the data.
events.rebuttal: The older colonial-era 'Aryan invasion' (a martial conquest wiping out the IVC) is not supported; the IVC declined for other reasons and Steppe ancestry arrived over centuries by admixture. But wholesale 'no migration at all / Out-of-India' claims are not supported by the ancient-DNA time-transects either. The honest statement: gene flow inward is real; 'invasion' is the wrong word; 'no migration' is also wrong.

source.label: Narasimhan et al. 2019, Science; and the surrounding scholarly debate

events.title: How related everyone is — the borders are younger than the blood
events.year_label: the through-line of the whole record
events.finding: Almost every living South Asian is a blend of the SAME three ancient sources (AASI + Iranian-farmer-related + Steppe), differing only in proportion. The very same Yamnaya/Steppe ancestry that entered South Asia also spread into Bronze-Age Europe — so North Indians and Europeans literally share a documented ancestral pulse. There is no genetically 'pure' or separate people here; the modern national and communal lines are far younger than the shared ancestry beneath them.
events.interpretation: This is the atlas's honest point: a DNA map shows how connected people are, not how divided. Borders drawn by 20th-century politics, and identities hardened by religion or nation, sit on top of a population that is deeply intermixed. The science does not endorse any 'us vs them' — it dissolves it. (What it does NOT do is license claims about any group being superior, indigenous-and-therefore-owning, or foreign-and-therefore-lesser — descent is not desert.)

source.label: Narasimhan et al. 2019, Science (shared Yamnaya ancestry in Europe & South Asia; ANI/ASI as blends of common sources)

events.title: Rakhigarhi genome ties living South Asians to the IVC
events.finding: The first (and so far only) sequenced Indus Valley genome, from a woman buried at Rakhigarhi, carried Iranian-related + AASI ancestry and NO Steppe or Anatolian-farmer ancestry — direct genetic continuity from the IVC to modern South Asians.
events.interpretation: The authors caution that this is a single individual, limiting firm conclusions. Links to the same Rakhigarhi site in the heritage atlas.
